Searched (en/ru terms) for any post-2010 revival of the Caspian Coastal / Prikaspiysky pipeline: none found. The newest independent evidence located is Eurasianet's 4 Jan 2016 piece on Gazprom formally suspending all Turkmen gas purchases, which states plainly of the 2007 deal that 'the promised pipeline never got built' — a working, independent, dated (2016) confirmation with no hint of revival, six years after the sheet's own CancelledYear=2010. No mentions of this project in later (2018-2026) Central Asian gas-pipeline coverage (TAPI, Central Asia-China expansions, East-West pipeline articles) that would suggest resurrection. Existing ShelvedCancelledType='confirmed' bookkeeping on the row is already complete and consistent with the evidence; no change proposed. Could not independently re-verify the exact CancelledYear=2010 date itself from a fresh working source: GEM's own cited Reuters piece (uk.reuters.com/article/idUKLDE69M02I20101023, 'Russia, Turkmenistan extend Caspian gas link freeze-paper') 401s as a bot-wall, and repeated Wayback Machine lookups in this session were rate-limited (HTTP 429) rather than resolving either way — so this is a tooling gap, not evidence against 2010. Circumstantial support for the ~2009-2010 timeframe is strong regardless (CACI Analyst documents the deal stalling from the Aug-2008 price crash through early 2009; Eurasianet notes Gazprom cut its 2010 Turkmen purchases to 10 bcm as relations soured).

Mothballed is still the right call, and it is now BETTER evidenced than before, not worse. Chain of dated evidence: (1) 2022-05-11 -- Ukraine's transmission operator (GTSOU) declared force majeure and stopped receiving gas at the Sokhranivka connection point / Novopskov compressor station in Russian-occupied Luhansk territory (RIA Novosti, Vedomosti, both 2022-05-10/11) -- Sokhranivka is Soyuz's own, specific Ukraine entry point, confirmed by en.wikipedia's Natural gas transmission system of Ukraine article ('enters Ukraine east of Novopskov through the Sokhranovka gas metering station'). (2) That same en.wikipedia article states that in 2023 only the Sudzha connection point (used by a different pipeline) was carrying Russian transit gas -- i.e. Soyuz-via-Sokhranovka carried none. (3) The whole Russia-Ukraine gas transit contract (covering all remaining routes, including any residual Soyuz capacity) expired at end of 2024 and transit fully stopped 2025-01-01 (Rossiyskaya Gazeta, 2025-01-01). So the pipeline's defining international-transit function has been non-operational continuously since 2022 and completely dead since Jan 2025 -- 'mothballed' (built, idle, theoretically resumable) fits better than 'operating', 'idle' (GEM's more informal/ambiguous variant), or 'retired' (nothing suggests permanent decommissioning/dismantlement). I could not find any source describing the physical state of the ~300 km Kazakh section specifically (e.g. whether it is used for any purely domestic or reverse-direction Kazakhstan gas movement independent of the Russia-Ukraine transit function) -- that remains an open, unresolved sub-question, noted here rather than papered over. Proposing ShelvedCancelledType='confirmed' (not 'inferred') because the 2022-05-11 halt is a specific, dated, sourced event, not merely GEM's no-progress dormancy rule; StopYear=2022 marks that first confirmed cessation of Soyuz's transit function. Flagging for the merge step that 'StopYear' vs 'ShelvedYear' as the correct column for a mothballed (as opposed to shelved/cancelled) built pipeline is not spelled out in the schema docs I have access to -- pick the column whose semantics matches 'year a built pipe stopped operating', currently believed to be StopYear.

EXISTENCE/STATUS: the underlying agreement is real, not a phantom entry. RFE/RL (12 May 2007, 'Central Asia: Russian, Turkmen, Kazakh Leaders Agree On Caspian Pipeline') is a contemporaneous, independent report of Putin/Berdymukhammedov/Nazarbaev's trilateral declaration to build a gas pipeline along the Caspian coast from Turkmenistan via Kazakhstan to Russia. Jamestown ('Turkmenistan, Natural Gas, and the West') independently corroborates the 12 Dec 2007 draft-agreement signing and the Belek->Alexandrov Gay route. CACI Analyst (8 Apr 2009, 'Moscow and Ashgabat Fail To Agree over the Caspian Coastal Pipeline') documents the deal stalling through 2008-2009 as gas prices crashed. Critically, Eurasianet ('Turkmenistan: Russia Suspends Gas Supplies', 4 Jan 2016) — a source with NO connection to GEM, published 6+ years after the sheet's CancelledYear — states in a retrospective that 'the promised pipeline never got built,' which is fresh, independent, working confirmation that cancelled/never-revived remains correct as of 2016, with no later evidence of revival found in any subsequent search (TAPI, Central Asia-China, and East-West pipeline coverage from 2015-2020 never mention a Caspian coastal revival). Verdict: 'cancelled' stands, corroborated by 2 independent sources (RFE/RL 2007 for the agreement's existence; Eurasianet 2016 for confirmed non-completion), tier=high.

resolutions.recommendation: Flag in ResearcherNotes (or check with Update) whether P0740 is meant to represent only the abandoned 2007-2010 expansion, or the whole physical corridor — and whether GGIT tracks the pre-existing CAC western-branch line elsewhere to avoid a hidden overlap.
resolutions.researcher_notes: CLASSIFICATION nuance not visible from the sheet: CACI Analyst (8 Apr 2009) states the 'Caspian Coastal Pipeline (CCP, also called by its Russian name the Prikaspii)... is part of the western branch of the Central Asia-Center (CAC) pipeline, a spidery network inherited from the Soviet era,' 'constructed over a third of a century ago,' and reportedly still carrying ~2 bcm/y (in disrepair) as of the article date after being 're-opened in the middle of the current decade' (i.e. mid-2000s). So this is NOT a wholly greenfield line: an existing, decades-old physical pipe already occupied this corridor before the 2007 agreement. The 2007-2010 story that GEM tracks (Belek->Alexandrov Gay, 20-30 bcm/y target, cancelled 2010) is specifically the REFURBISHMENT/CAPACITY-EXPANSION project layered onto that old line (CACI: 'this would include an upgrade of the existing CCP where feasible... [plus] construction of an offshore pipeline to carry an additional 10 bcm/y'). 'Cancelled' is the right verdict for that expansion — it never proceeded past agreements/declarations, confirmed by Eurasianet's 'never got built.' But if the GEM row is implicitly meant to describe the whole named corridor rather than just the increment, a reader could wrongly infer no pipe exists on this route at all, when in fact a legacy Soviet-era line reportedly continued operating (at reduced volume) on the same alignment. This project's roster (P0740, P0761) doesn't include a separate 'Central Asia-Center' entity to check for a duplicate/overlap directly — routing this as a classification flag rather than resolving it here.

resolutions.researcher_notes: The recorded Capacity (25.00 bcm/y) does not clearly match any single figure in the primary reporting, and the underlying figures conflict across the plan's own history. CACI Analyst (8 Apr 2009) reports Putin's original 2007 proposal as 'a pipeline to carry 30 bcm/y along the land route, of which the first stage... would foresee at least 10 bcm/y that Russia would commit to purchase,' PLUS a separate 'offshore pipeline to carry an additional 10 bcm/y.' Jamestown corroborates the 10 bcm/y first-stage purchase commitment specifically ('up to 10 billion cubic meters of Turkmen gas annually'). So the sourced numbers are 10 (near-term commitment), 30 (announced land-route target), and up to 40 (land+offshore) bcm/y — not 25. The 20-30 bcm/y range (and the sheet's apparent midpoint of that range) appears in later secondary/aggregator summaries but I could not find an independent primary source stating 25 bcm/y specifically; the figure looks like an unsourced smoothing of a range rather than a corroborated data point. Flagging as a material spec disagreement rather than silently passing it; not forcing a replacement number since none of the individually-cited figures (10/30/40) is unambiguously 'the' right one for a single Capacity field either.

resolutions.recommendation: No action on existence/route. Real, well-documented Soviet-era export trunk line (Orenburg RU -> Uralsk KZ -> Aleksandrov Gai RU -> Sokhranovka/Novopskov -> Kremenchug/Dolyna UA -> Uzhgorod), built 1975-79, in service from 1980. It genuinely has a Kazakh section (~300 km, via Uralsk) -- this is not a GEM-only or phantom entity.
resolutions.researcher_notes: Checked whether this pipeline physically exists and actually transits Kazakhstan (the sheet's own gem.wiki citation list is almost entirely Russian/Ukrainian-language secondary sources, none of them GEM-derived, which is itself a healthy sign). Independently confirmed via ru.wikipedia.org, neftegaz.ru (Russian technical library, 2014), fb.ru, and a 2021 Sputnik news report on a pipeline-rupture-driven transit halt: all four describe the same route Orenburg (Orenburg Oblast, Russia) -> Uralsk (West Kazakhstan) -> Aleksandrov Gai (Russia) -> Ukraine border -> Uzhgorod, built by USSR + Comecon countries 1975-79, commissioned 1980. The 2021 Sputnik piece additionally corroborates it as a live, physically real, operating asset as of Feb 2021 (an actual pipeline rupture near Mukhranova, Orenburg Oblast, forced an emergency halt of transit to Kazakhstan). No duplicate concern versus the only other in-scope row (P0740, Caspian Coastal Gas Pipeline) -- that is an unrelated, never-built, cancelled Russia-Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan littoral project, not the same physical pipe.

resolutions.researcher_notes: The live GEM CSV (data/GGIT_gas.csv) has PipelineNetworkGrouping = 'Brotherhood pipeline system' for P0761. This is wrong. 'Brotherhood' (Bratstvo) is the standard English name for the Urengoy-Pomary-Uzhhorod pipeline (also called West-Siberian/Trans-Siberian pipeline) -- a SEPARATE ~4,500 km system originating at the Urengoy field in Siberia, not at Orenburg. en.wikipedia's Urengoy-Pomary-Uzhhorod article confirms it is 'also known as the Bratstvo pipeline, Brotherhood pipeline' and that it 'runs alongside' the Soyuz pipeline as a distinct, parallel system. neftegaz.ru's own Soyuz writeup independently corroborates the separateness: it says Soyuz 'connects with' ('соединяется с') the Urengoy-Pomary-Uzhhorod and Progress trunk lines at the city of Bar -- language that only makes sense if they are different pipelines meeting at a junction, not one system. Two independent sources agree Brotherhood != Soyuz. This looks like a genuine grouping/classification error on the GEM side, worth fixing via Update.
